card.official_title: Speed Up Street Safety Projects, Disposition of Unused City Property, Office Leasing
card.plain_title: Change reviews for street projects, city property, and office space
card.put_on_ballot_by: Not identified in the official guide's summary.
card.yes_means: A yes vote changes review rules for street projects, shortens review for certain city property transactions, and removes hearing and approval requirements for city office space.
card.no_means: A no vote keeps existing street-project consultation rules, city property review procedures, and the Council's power to reject city office acquisitions or leases.

what_changes.today: DOT must notify local officials and Community Boards and consult police, fire, disability, and small-business offices before major transportation projects.
what_changes.if_passes: DOT's authority to begin urgent, data-backed safety work before notification is clarified, and technical errors or missed consultations cannot stop a project.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Most city property sales or leases undergo a seven-month land-use review with City Council review.
what_changes.if_passes: Smaller lots and development rights at city-owned landmarks can receive shorter review ending with the Planning Commission, if no environmental impact statement is required.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: A program allows sales of undevelopable city lots to neighboring owners without public auction.
what_changes.if_passes: That authority becomes permanent on December 31, 2030.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: A public hearing is required when more than two years pass after Council approval of a property sale or acquisition.
what_changes.if_passes: That additional public hearing is no longer required.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Office acquisitions or leases require a Planning Commission hearing and vote, with Council review and rejection possible by a two-thirds vote.
what_changes.if_passes: The city administrative services commissioner certifies acquisitions instead, with local advance notice but no Planning Commission or Council approval or hearings.
what_changes.label: fact

who_is_affected: People using streets affected by bike lanes, bus lanes, or road redesigns
Residents and Community Boards near affected city properties
Owners of property next to undevelopable city lots
City employees and agencies using city office space
City Council members, Borough Presidents, and the City Planning Commission

fiscal_impact.text: The official guide does not include a cost estimate.
fiscal_impact.label: fact

steelman_yes.headline: Urgent, data-backed street safety work should not be stopped by technical errors or missed consultations.
more_reasons: For eligible property transactions, shorter review keeps Community Board and Borough President input while removing a final Council review.
For office space, commissioner certification and notice replace hearings and approval steps.

best_evidence.text: Technical errors or missed consultations would no longer be valid reasons to stop a transportation project.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: The shorter property review allows Community Boards and Borough Presidents to review proposals at the same time, with a final Planning Commission decision.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: People waiting on urgent street safety work, and agencies handling City property and office deals.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: The trade-off is fewer approval steps, not the removal of all local input: eligible property transactions retain local review, and office acquisitions retain advance notice.

steelman_no.headline: City property decisions should retain final Council review rather than end with the Planning Commission.
more_reasons: Keeping office-space rules preserves a public hearing and the Council's power to reject an acquisition or lease.
Keeping street-project rules preserves missed consultation as a possible basis for stopping a project.

best_evidence.text: Eligible property transactions would no longer receive final City Council review.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Current office-space rules include a Planning Commission public hearing and allow the Council to disapprove by a two-thirds vote.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Residents who value public hearings and a final review by elected officials of City property and office decisions.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Urgent safety work is only one part of the proposal; keeping the current rules also preserves separate oversight of city property and office transactions.

crux.text: The central trade-off is fewer procedural barriers versus stronger public and elected-official oversight. The proposal combines street safety rules with separate changes to city property and office-space decisions.

evidence.text: The street provision clarifies existing authority for immediate action in limited safety cases supported by data; it does not broadly remove notification requirements.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Shorter property review is limited to specified transactions that do not require an environmental impact statement.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: For office acquisitions, local officials and the Community Board receive advance notice; the Council and Comptroller receive notice after the acquisition is final.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Most changes take effect upon certification of voter approval; permanent authority for undevelopable-lot sales begins December 31, 2030.
evidence.label: fact

turing_yes.reason: The Yes case fairly emphasizes the proposal’s limited, data-backed authority for urgent street-safety work and the procedural efficiencies in property and office decisions. It could state the expected benefit of shorter project timelines more directly, but it is not a strawman.

turing_no.reason: The No case fairly presents the trade-off as reduced public and elected-official oversight, citing the removal of final Council review for eligible property transactions and hearings and Council disapproval authority for office space. It gives a thoughtful account of the main oversight concern.

swap_notes: The headlines use parallel “Analysis-based case for/against” framing and similarly measured language. They emphasize different parts of a proposal covering several topics—street safety for Yes and property review for No—but neither is materially warmer or more confident.
